summary: A republication of PKCS #9 version 2.0 from RSA Laboratories, selecting object classes and attribute types for use in other PKCS standards. Change control remains within the PKCS process.

plainLanguage.summary: PKCS #9 defines names and data types for information used in public-key documents and directories. RFC 2985 republishes version 2.0 of the specification, while its change control remains within the PKCS process.

subtitle: A set of directory classes and attribute definitions used with public-key standards.

tldr.problem: Public-key formats and directory services need shared definitions for the information they store and exchange.
tldr.mechanism: PKCS #9 version 2.0 defines two auxiliary object classes, attribute types for several PKCS formats, and matching rules, with ASN.1 definitions and an LDAP-oriented BNF summary.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2985 republishes the RSA Laboratories PKCS #9 v2.0 specification as an Informational memo. Change control remains within the PKCS process.

today: RFC 2985 is an Informational memo published in November 2000. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the RFC states that change control remains within the PKCS process.

sections.title: What PKCS #9 Defines
sections.content:
This memo republishes PKCS #9 version 2.0 from RSA Laboratories. Apart from the security considerations section, its body is taken directly from that specification, and change control remains within the PKCS process.

It defines object classes, attribute types and matching rules for use with public-key cryptography and LDAP-accessible directories. Its definitions cover PKCS #7 signed messages, PKCS #10 certificate requests, PKCS #12 personal information exchanges and PKCS #15 cryptographic tokens.
sections.plainLanguage: PKCS #9 gives consistent names and data types for information used by public-key formats and directories. This RFC republishes version 2.0 rather than creating a new Internet standard.

sections.title: Two Auxiliary Object Classes
sections.content:
An auxiliary object class adds optional attributes to a directory entry. pkcsEntity is for PKCS-related data, including a PKCS #7 ContentInfo, a PKCS #12 PFX, a PKCS #15 token and encrypted private-key information.

naturalPerson is for information about people. Its attributes include email address, unstructured name and address, date and place of birth, gender, citizenship, residence, pseudonym and serial number. The country attributes use two-letter country codes, and the gender value is one letter, M or F in either case.
sections.plainLanguage: pkcsEntity can add attributes for cryptographic data to a directory entry. naturalPerson can add personal details such as a name, email address or date of birth.

sections.title: Attributes for Signed Data
sections.content:
PKCS #7 signed data can include attributes such as contentType, messageDigest and signingTime. If authenticated attributes are present, contentType and messageDigest are required. The signing-time value states when the signer purportedly signed, but the recipient decides whether to accept it.

A signer unable or unwilling to provide a time may use a randomNonce or sequenceNumber; the memo says these can help protect against replay attacks when used correctly. A counterSignature signs another signature and is an unauthenticated attribute. A countersignature may itself contain another countersignature.
sections.plainLanguage: Attributes can identify signed content, give its digest and record a claimed signing time. A nonce or sequence number can help detect replay, and a countersignature signs another signature.

sections.title: Requests, Stored Keys and Matching
sections.content:
For PKCS #10 certificate requests, challengePassword is a password an entity may use to request certificate revocation, and extensionRequest carries certificate extensions requested by the applicant. The memo deprecates extendedCertificateAttributes because PKCS #6 became historic after X.509 version 3 certificates.

For PKCS #12 and PKCS #15, friendlyName gives an object a user-friendly name and localKeyId identifies a key locally within an application. The matching rules include a case-insensitive string comparison and a rule for comparing signing times.
sections.plainLanguage: Certificate requests and stored keys have attributes for requested extensions, a challenge password, a local key identifier and a readable name. Matching rules tell directory software when two attribute values count as equal.

sections.title: Privacy and Stored Values
sections.content:
Directory attributes can describe people, organizations and devices. The RFC notes that many countries have privacy laws about publishing personal information, and says challengePassword should not be stored unencrypted in a directory.

Attributes of pkcsEntity may be readable by third parties and should be protected. If a password-protected PKCS value is stored, the directory should authenticate a requester before delivering it to reduce the risk of an offline password-search attack.
sections.plainLanguage: Some directory attributes contain personal information or protected keys. The RFC advises against storing a challenge password unencrypted and recommends checking requesters before returning password-protected values.
